Lab 6: Binary Outcomes and Maximum Likelihood

Intermediate Quantitative Methods · Week 6

Author

Sebastian Ramirez-Ruiz

Term

Autumn 2026

Welcome! 👋

This week’s seminar was about outcomes that are switches: voted or not, radical right or not, request affirmed or not. We saw three models for them (the LPM, logit, and probit), learned to read a logit coefficient with care, turned models into quantities people understand, and closed with the logic of maximum likelihood. Today we do all of it in R. The lab has three parts, plus an optional fourth:

  • First, we write a likelihood by hand and maximize it: for six voters, then for a logit with thousands.
  • Second, we fit the LPM, logit, and probit to a survey of radical-right voting and ask the models for predictions, comparisons, and slopes with {marginaleffects}, first by hand, then with the package.
  • Third, we look at an interaction on two scales, with a simulated audit of local health offices.
  • Fourth, optional and on your own: we watch non-collapsibility happen, in a table and in a simulation. Martín will not cover this part in the lab.

Along the way, we practice the R skills from Labs 4 and 5 (writing functions, iterating with {purrr}, building grids with tidyr::expand_grid()) and add two new ones: maximizing a function with optim(), and computing counterfactual predictions by changing a column and predicting again.

As in the last two labs, every data set is simulated, so we know the truth and can check whether the models recover it.

Plan for today ≈ time
Maximum likelihood by hand: six voters, then a logit 30 min
LPM, logit, probit; predictions, comparisons, and slopes 40 min
An interaction on two scales: the audit 30 min
Wrap-up 10 min

Packages 📦

# Install these in your CONSOLE if you have not done so yet:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "marginaleffects", "sandwich"))

library(tidyverse) # data wrangling and plots; loads {dplyr}, {tidyr}, {purrr}, {ggplot2}
library(marginaleffects) # predictions, comparisons, and slopes from fitted models

{sandwich} is used once, behind the scenes, when we ask {marginaleffects} for robust standard errors. We do not load it.

Part I: Maximum likelihood by hand ✍️

Six voters 🗳

Six voters from one small town. Two voted for the radical-right party (coded 1), four for other parties (coded 0). If each voter picks the party with the same probability \(p\), how probable is this exact pattern of votes?

Each voter contributes a factor: \(p\) if they voted radical right, \(1 - p\) if not. Voters decide independently, so we multiply:

\[\mathcal{L}(p) = \prod_{i=1}^{6} p^{\,y_i}(1-p)^{\,1-y_i}\]

As a function in R:

votes <- c(0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0)

lik_p <- function(p, y) {
  prod(p^y * (1 - p)^(1 - y))
}

lik_p(0.2, y = votes) # = 0.2^2 * 0.8^4
[1] 0.016384
lik_p(0.5, y = votes)
[1] 0.015625

The probability reading fixes \(p\) and asks about the data. The likelihood reading fixes the data and varies \(p\). So let’s try many values of \(p\) and keep the best:

lik_grid <- tibble::tibble(p = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(L = purrr::map_dbl(p, lik_p, y = votes))

lik_grid %>% dplyr::slice_max(L, n = 1)
ggplot(lik_grid, aes(p, L)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "#1d375b") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1 / 3, linetype = "dashed", color = "#c6273b") +
  labs(x = "Radical-right vote share p", y = "Likelihood of these six votes") +
  theme_minimal()

The peak sits at \(\hat p = 2/6\): the maximum likelihood estimate is simply the share who voted radical right.

Logs, and letting R climb 🧗

Products of many small numbers quickly become too small for a computer to store. Logs turn products into sums and keep the same peak. dbinom(y, 1, p, log = TRUE) returns \(\log\big(p^{y}(1-p)^{1-y}\big)\) for each voter:

loglik_p <- function(p, y) {
  sum(dbinom(y, size = 1, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

loglik_p(1 / 3, y = votes)
[1] -3.819085
log(lik_p(1 / 3, y = votes)) # the same number
[1] -3.819085

Instead of a grid, we let R search. For a single parameter, optimize() finds the maximum on an interval:

optimize(loglik_p, interval = c(0.001, 0.999), y = votes, maximum = TRUE)
$maximum
[1] 0.3333252

$objective
[1] -3.819085

Activity 💡

  1. Now take 60 voters with the same share: votes_60 <- rep(votes, 10). Find the maximum likelihood estimate with optimize(). Is it different?
  2. Plot the log-likelihood of both samples over p from 0.05 to 0.75, each shifted so that its maximum is 0 (subtract the maximum). Which curve is sharper?
  3. The standard error comes from that sharpness: \(\text{SE} \approx 1/\sqrt{-\ell''(\hat p)}\). Approximate the second derivative at \(\hat p\) with a finite difference, \(\ell''(p) \approx \big[\ell(p + h) - 2\ell(p) + \ell(p - h)\big]/h^2\) with \(h = 0.001\), and compute the SE for both samples. Compare with the textbook formula \(\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}\).
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
# 1.
votes_60 <- rep(votes, 10)
optimize(loglik_p, interval = c(0.001, 0.999), y = votes_60, maximum = TRUE)
$maximum
[1] 0.3333252

$objective
[1] -38.19085
# 2.
ll_curves <- tidyr::expand_grid(p = seq(0.05, 0.75, by = 0.005),
                                sample = c("2 of 6", "20 of 60")) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(ll = purrr::map2_dbl(p, sample, \(p, s) {
    loglik_p(p, y = if (s == "2 of 6") votes else votes_60)
  })) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(sample) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(ll = ll - max(ll)) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup()

ggplot(ll_curves, aes(p, ll, color = sample)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-8, 0.3)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#6B8CB8", "#1d375b")) +
  labs(x = "p", y = "Log-likelihood (relative to its maximum)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
# 3.
se_from_curvature <- function(y, h = 0.001) {
  p_hat <- mean(y)
  second <- (loglik_p(p_hat + h, y) - 2 * loglik_p(p_hat, y) + loglik_p(p_hat - h, y)) / h^2
  1 / sqrt(-second)
}

tibble::tibble(
  sample = c("2 of 6", "20 of 60"),
  se_curvature = c(se_from_curvature(votes), se_from_curvature(votes_60)),
  se_formula = c(sqrt((1/3) * (2/3) / 6), sqrt((1/3) * (2/3) / 60))
)
  1. The estimate is the same, 1/3: the peak depends only on the share.
  2. The 60-voter curve is much sharper: values of \(p\) away from 1/3 make 60 votes far less likely than they make 6 votes.
  3. The curvature gives the same standard errors as the formula you know: about 0.19 with 6 voters and 0.06 with 60. Ten times the data, \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2\) times the precision.

A logit, by hand 📈

A regression gives each person their own probability. For a logit with one predictor, \(p_i = \Lambda(\alpha + \beta x_i)\), where \(\Lambda\) is the logistic function (plogis() in R). The log-likelihood is the same sum as before, with a different \(p_i\) for each person.

First, the survey from the seminar: 3,000 voters, anti-immigration attitudes on a 0–10 scale, sex, a university degree, rural residence, and age. As in previous labs, we write the simulation as a function:

make_survey <- function(n = 3000) {
  tibble::tibble(degree = rbinom(n, 1, 0.35),
                 male = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
                 rural = rbinom(n, 1, 0.3),
                 age = round(runif(n, 18, 85))) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      immig = pmin(pmax(round(5.3 - 1.3 * degree + 0.6 * rural + 2.2 * rnorm(n)), 0), 10),
      rrv = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-5.8 + 0.62 * immig + 0.5 * male - 0.45 * degree +
                                  0.3 * rural - 0.008 * (age - 50)))
    )
}

survey <- make_survey()
mean(survey$rrv) # share voting radical right
[1] 0.1403333

Now the log-likelihood of a logit with one predictor. beta holds the two parameters, \((\alpha, \beta)\):

loglik_logit <- function(beta, y, x) {
  p <- plogis(beta[1] + beta[2] * x)
  sum(dbinom(y, size = 1, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

loglik_logit(c(0, 0), y = survey$rrv, x = survey$immig) # a flat curve at p = 0.5
[1] -2079.442
loglik_logit(c(-5, 0.6), y = survey$rrv, x = survey$immig) # a much better candidate
[1] -974.5787

With two parameters we use optim(). By default it minimizes, so fnscale = -1 tells it to maximize. hessian = TRUE returns the curvature at the top, which gives the standard errors:

ml_fit <- optim(par = c(0, 0), fn = loglik_logit,
                y = survey$rrv, x = survey$immig,
                method = "BFGS", control = list(fnscale = -1), hessian = TRUE)

ml_fit$par # the estimates
[1] -5.7140747  0.6430378
sqrt(diag(solve(-ml_fit$hessian))) # their standard errors
[1] 0.23062806 0.03279827

And the same model with glm():

glm_fit <- glm(rrv ~ immig, data = survey, family = binomial)
summary(glm_fit)$coefficients[, 1:2]
             Estimate Std. Error
(Intercept) -5.714077 0.23062587
immig        0.643038 0.03279787

Same estimates, same standard errors. That is what glm() does under the hood (with a faster climbing algorithm: the “Fisher Scoring iterations” at the bottom of summary()).

Activity 💡

  1. Write loglik_logit_X(beta, y, X), a version that takes a matrix of predictors X (with a column of 1s for the intercept) and computes \(p_i = \Lambda(X_i\beta)\) with X %*% beta. Build X with model.matrix(~ immig + male, data = survey) and maximize it with optim(), starting from zeros. Compare with glm(rrv ~ immig + male, ...).
  2. Turn it into a probit by changing one function. Compare with glm(..., family = binomial(link = "probit")).
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
# 1.
loglik_logit_X <- function(beta, y, X) {
  p <- plogis(as.vector(X %*% beta))
  sum(dbinom(y, size = 1, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

X <- model.matrix(~ immig + male, data = survey)
ml_fit2 <- optim(par = rep(0, ncol(X)), fn = loglik_logit_X, y = survey$rrv, X = X,
                 method = "BFGS", control = list(fnscale = -1))
ml_fit2$par
[1] -6.0359606  0.6475714  0.5483103
coef(glm(rrv ~ immig + male, data = survey, family = binomial))
(Intercept)       immig        male 
 -6.0359906   0.6475756   0.5483116 
# 2. the probit: pnorm() instead of plogis()
loglik_probit_X <- function(beta, y, X) {
  p <- pnorm(as.vector(X %*% beta))
  sum(dbinom(y, size = 1, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

ml_probit <- optim(par = rep(0, ncol(X)), fn = loglik_probit_X, y = survey$rrv, X = X,
                   method = "BFGS", control = list(fnscale = -1))
ml_probit$par
[1] -3.3363490  0.3521976  0.3103786
coef(glm(rrv ~ immig + male, data = survey, family = binomial(link = "probit")))
(Intercept)       immig        male 
 -3.3363706   0.3522007   0.3103801
  1. The estimates match glm() up to small numerical differences. Nothing about the function needed to change except how \(p_i\) is computed: the “recipe” of maximum likelihood is always the same.
  2. Only the link changes: pnorm() (the normal curve) instead of plogis() (the logistic curve). The probit coefficients are smaller, by a factor of roughly 1.6 to 1.8, because the two curves assume errors with different spreads. That is why you should never compare a logit coefficient with a probit one.

Part II: LPM, logit, probit, and the quantities we care about 🎯

Three models, three languages 🗣

fit_lpm <- lm(rrv ~ immig + male + degree + rural + age, data = survey)
fit_logit <- glm(rrv ~ immig + male + degree + rural + age, data = survey, family = binomial)
fit_probit <- glm(rrv ~ immig + male + degree + rural + age, data = survey,
                  family = binomial(link = "probit"))

tibble::tibble(term = names(coef(fit_lpm)),
               LPM = coef(fit_lpm),
               Logit = coef(fit_logit),
               Probit = coef(fit_probit))

Three numbers for male, three meanings: a change in the probability (LPM), in the log-odds (logit), and in a latent index (probit). To compare them, we need the same quantity from each model.

Predictions 🔮

The simplest question to ask a fitted model: what does it expect for someone with given characteristics? marginaleffects::datagrid() builds the profile; the other variables are held at their means (or modes):

marginaleffects::predictions(fit_logit,
  newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(immig = c(4, 7), male = 1, degree = 0, rural = 1, age = 45))

 immig male degree rural age Estimate Pr(>|z|)     S  2.5 % 97.5 %
     4    1      0     1  45   0.0756   <0.001 198.8 0.0571 0.0993
     7    1      0     1  45   0.3499   <0.001  22.9 0.2995 0.4038

Type: invlink(link)

The same question for every value of attitudes, and for all three models. purrr::map() runs the same function on each model, and purrr::list_rbind() stacks the results:

models <- list(LPM = fit_lpm, Logit = fit_logit, Probit = fit_probit)

curves <- models %>%
  purrr::map(\(m) marginaleffects::predictions(m,
    newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(model = m, immig = seq(0, 10, by = 0.25),
                                        male = 1, degree = 0, rural = 1, age = 45)) %>%
      tibble::as_tibble()) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind(names_to = "model")

ggplot(curves, aes(immig, estimate, color = model)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = 0, fill = "#fdf0f1") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(LPM = "#c6273b", Logit = "#1d375b", Probit = "#639E7D")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Anti-immigration attitudes (0-10)", y = "P(votes radical right)", color = NULL,
       subtitle = "A 45-year-old rural man without a degree") +
  theme_minimal()

The logit and probit curves are almost the same. The LPM is a straight line, and it goes below 0.

Activity 💡

  1. What share of the 3,000 respondents get an LPM prediction below 0 or above 1? (Hint: fitted(fit_lpm).)
  2. Where do the three models agree most, and where do they disagree? Answer by looking at the plot, then check with predictions at immig = 0, 5, and 10.
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
# 1.
mean(fitted(fit_lpm) < 0 | fitted(fit_lpm) > 1)
[1] 0.172
# 2.
curves %>%
  dplyr::filter(immig %in% c(0, 5, 10)) %>%
  dplyr::select(model, immig, estimate) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = estimate)
  1. A sizable share of respondents get impossible probabilities, all of them below 0: voters with liberal views on immigration, for whom the line runs past the floor.
  2. The three agree in the middle of the scale, where most voters are. They part ways at the ends: the LPM is too low (even negative) for the most liberal voters, and its straight line misses how fast support rises among the most opposed.

Comparisons, by hand and with the package ⚖️

What is the gender gap in the probability of voting radical right? With a logit, there is no single number in the table that answers this. But we can ask the model:

  1. Predict for every respondent as if they were a man.
  2. Predict for every respondent as if they were a woman.
  3. Take the difference for each person, and average.

These are counterfactual predictions: we change one column and predict again.

p_men <- predict(fit_logit, newdata = dplyr::mutate(survey, male = 1), type = "response")
p_women <- predict(fit_logit, newdata = dplyr::mutate(survey, male = 0), type = "response")

mean(p_men - p_women) # the average marginal effect (AME) of being male
[1] 0.05268225

{marginaleffects} does exactly this, and adds a standard error:

marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit_logit, variables = "male")

 Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S  2.5 % 97.5 %
   0.0527     0.0112 4.69   <0.001 18.5 0.0307 0.0747

Term: male
Type: response
Comparison: 1 - 0

Activity 💡

  1. Compute the same AME for the LPM and the probit with marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(), and put the three in one table. For the LPM, ask for robust standard errors with vcov = "HC2" (the LPM is heteroskedastic by construction).
  2. The AME averages 3,000 individual gaps. Plot their distribution: p_men - p_women from the code above. Why are they not all the same in a logit? Would they be in the LPM?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
# 1.
dplyr::bind_rows(
  LPM = marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit_lpm, variables = "male", vcov = "HC2") %>% tibble::as_tibble(),
  Logit = marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit_logit, variables = "male") %>% tibble::as_tibble(),
  Probit = marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit_probit, variables = "male") %>% tibble::as_tibble(),
  .id = "model"
) %>%
  dplyr::select(model, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)
# 2.
tibble::tibble(gap = p_men - p_women) %>%
  ggplot(aes(100 * gap)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#1d375b") +
  labs(x = "Gender gap for each respondent (percentage points)", y = "Respondents") +
  theme_minimal()
  1. The three models give very similar average gaps, a few percentage points. They target the same quantity, so they are comparable, unlike the three coefficients.
  2. In a logit, the effect of being male on the probability depends on where a person sits on the curve: tiny for someone whose probability is near 0, larger for someone closer to the middle. In the LPM, the gap is the coefficient, the same for everyone, by assumption.

Slopes, and whether they differ across groups 📐

For a continuous predictor, the question is a slope: how fast does the probability rise for a little more anti-immigration sentiment? Averaged over all respondents, this is the average marginal effect of attitudes, in percentage points per point on the 0–10 scale:

marginaleffects::avg_slopes(fit_logit, variables = "immig")

 Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)     S  2.5 % 97.5 %
   0.0589     0.0026 22.6   <0.001 373.9 0.0538  0.064

Term: immig
Type: response
Comparison: dY/dX
coef(fit_lpm)["immig"] # the LPM's one slope for everyone
    immig 
0.0599733

Now group the voters by their attitudes and average the slopes within each group. The grouping does not change the model; it only says over whom to average:

survey_grp <- survey %>%
  dplyr::mutate(attitudes = cut(immig, breaks = c(-1, 3, 6, 10),
                                labels = c("Low (0-3)", "Middle (4-6)", "High (7-10)")))

marginaleffects::avg_slopes(fit_logit, variables = "immig", newdata = survey_grp, by = "attitudes")

    attitudes Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)     S   2.5 % 97.5 %
 Low (0-3)      0.0089   0.000911  9.77   <0.001  72.4 0.00712 0.0107
 Middle (4-6)   0.0464   0.002295 20.23   <0.001 300.0 0.04194 0.0509
 High (7-10)    0.1285   0.007210 17.83   <0.001 233.8 0.11441 0.1427

Term: immig
Type: response
Comparison: dY/dX

Is the slope steeper among the most opposed than among the least opposed? Test the difference directly. b1, b2, b3 refer to the rows in the order printed above:

marginaleffects::avg_slopes(fit_logit, variables = "immig", newdata = survey_grp, by = "attitudes",
                            hypothesis = "b3 - b1 = 0")

 Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)     S 2.5 % 97.5 %
    b3-b1=0     0.12    0.00778 15.4   <0.001 174.8 0.104  0.135

Type: response

None of this is legible from the coefficient table, where attitudes have a single number.

Activity 💡

  1. A slope is the steepness of the curve at one spot. Approximate the slope at each respondent’s own values by hand: predict at immig and at immig + 0.001, take the difference, and divide by 0.001. Average it, and compare with marginaleffects::avg_slopes().
  2. Is the gender gap the same among graduates and non-graduates? Use marginaleffects::avg_comparisons() with by = "degree", then test the difference. Note that the model has no sex × degree interaction. Where does the difference come from?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
# 1.
h <- 0.001
p_here <- predict(fit_logit, newdata = survey, type = "response")
p_nudged <- predict(fit_logit, newdata = dplyr::mutate(survey, immig = immig + h), type = "response")
mean((p_nudged - p_here) / h)
[1] 0.05891606
# 2.
marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit_logit, variables = "male", by = "degree")

 degree Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S  2.5 % 97.5 %
      0   0.0622    0.01327 4.69   <0.001 18.5 0.0362 0.0882
      1   0.0346    0.00776 4.46   <0.001 16.9 0.0194 0.0498

Term: male
Type: response
Comparison: 1 - 0
marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit_logit, variables = "male", by = "degree",
                                 hypothesis = "b2 - b1 = 0")

 Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 %  97.5 %
    b2-b1=0  -0.0276    0.00667 -4.15   <0.001 14.9 -0.0407 -0.0146

Type: response
  1. The finite difference reproduces avg_slopes(): a slope is just a comparison for a very small change.
  2. The gap is smaller among graduates, and the difference is statistically distinguishable from zero, even though the model has no interaction term. In a logit, the effect on the probability depends on where people sit on the curve: graduates are less likely to vote radical right to begin with, so the same log-odds effect moves their probability less. Whether this counts as “an interaction” depends on the scale you have in mind, which is the topic of Part III.

Part III: An interaction on two scales 🔁

A simulated audit 📞

The seminar’s audit, in the spirit of Schaeffer et al. (2026, APSR): callers whose accent sounds native-Italian or West-African ask municipal health offices to register them with a family doctor. Is the gap larger in towns with a far-right mayor? Our simulation keeps the question but not their design (they combine the audit with a close-election regression discontinuity).

make_audit <- function(n = 1000, b0 = 4.6, b_accent = -2.1, b_mayor = -0.2, b_inter = -1.1) {
  tibble::tibble(farright = rbinom(n, 1, 0.4),
                 west_african = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
                 female = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)) %>% # the caller's gender also varied, as in the study
    dplyr::mutate(affirmed = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(b0 + b_accent * west_african + b_mayor * farright +
                                                   b_inter * west_african * farright)))
}

set.seed(66) # the same simulated audit as in the seminar slides
audit <- make_audit()
fit_aud <- glm(affirmed ~ west_african * farright, data = audit, family = binomial)

First, the four predicted rates:

marginaleffects::avg_predictions(fit_aud, by = c("west_african", "farright"))

 west_african farright Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)     S 2.5 % 97.5 %
            0        0    0.984    0.00722 136.2   <0.001   Inf 0.970  0.998
            0        1    0.985    0.00868 113.5   <0.001   Inf 0.968  1.002
            1        0    0.905    0.01712  52.8   <0.001   Inf 0.871  0.938
            1        1    0.741    0.03089  24.0   <0.001 420.4 0.681  0.802

Type: response

Is the gap larger under far-right mayors? 🔍

On the log-odds scale, the answer is the interaction coefficient, as you would see in the coefficient table:

summary(fit_aud)$coefficients["west_african:farright", ]
  Estimate Std. Error    z value   Pr(>|z|) 
-1.2719872  0.7790022 -1.6328417  0.1025023

On the probability scale, the answer is the difference between the two gaps, which we ask the model for:

marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit_aud, variables = "west_african", by = "farright")

 farright Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)    S  2.5 %  97.5 %
        0   -0.079     0.0186 -4.25   <0.001 15.5 -0.115 -0.0425
        1   -0.244     0.0321 -7.59   <0.001 44.8 -0.306 -0.1807

Term: west_african
Type: response
Comparison: 1 - 0
marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit_aud, variables = "west_african", by = "farright",
                                 hypothesis = "b2 - b1 = 0")

 Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)    S  2.5 %  97.5 %
    b2-b1=0   -0.165     0.0371 -4.44   <0.001 16.8 -0.237 -0.0919

Type: response

Adding type = "link" asks for the same comparisons on the log-odds scale. The difference between the gaps is then exactly the interaction coefficient:

marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit_aud, variables = "west_african", by = "farright",
                                 type = "link", hypothesis = "b2 - b1 = 0")

 Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)   S 2.5 % 97.5 %
    b2-b1=0    -1.27      0.779 -1.63    0.103 3.3  -2.8  0.255

Type: link

Same model, same data, two questions, and here they disagree. Native-Italian-sounding callers are affirmed almost always, and near the ceiling their log-odds rest on a handful of refusals, so the interaction coefficient is estimated imprecisely.

⚠️ Neither scale is “correct”. Choose the one that matches your question before you look at the results. For “how many more callers are turned away”, that is the probability scale. Report the logit interaction only if your question is about odds ratios, and say so.

Activity 💡

  1. Fit a linear probability model with the same interaction: lm(affirmed ~ west_african * farright, data = audit). Compare its interaction coefficient with the difference in gaps on the probability scale. Why are they (almost) the same here?
  2. Does the disagreement depend on where the rates sit? Write a function both_tests(d) that fits the logit to an audit d and returns the p-values of the two tests. Then run 100 simulated audits for each baseline b0 = c(4.6, 2.5, 1) (keep everything else, including the interaction of −1.1 on the log-odds scale) and compute how often each test rejects at the 5% level. (Hint: tidyr::expand_grid() and purrr::map(), as in Part I.)
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
# 1.
lpm_aud <- lm(affirmed ~ west_african * farright, data = audit)
coef(lpm_aud)["west_african:farright"]
west_african:farright 
           -0.1646035 
marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit_aud, variables = "west_african", by = "farright",
                                 hypothesis = "b2 - b1 = 0")$estimate
[1] -0.1646035
# 2.
both_tests <- function(d) {
  fit <- glm(affirmed ~ west_african * farright, data = d, family = binomial)
  pp <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit, variables = "west_african", by = "farright",
                                         hypothesis = "b2 - b1 = 0")
  tibble::tibble(p_logodds = summary(fit)$coefficients["west_african:farright", 4],
                 p_pp = pp$p.value)
}

rejections <- tidyr::expand_grid(b0 = c(4.6, 2.5, 1), rep = 1:100) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(res = purrr::map(b0, \(b) both_tests(make_audit(b0 = b)))) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(res) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(b0) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(reject_logodds = mean(p_logodds < 0.05),
                   reject_pp = mean(p_pp < 0.05))
rejections
  1. With two binary variables and their interaction, both models are saturated: each reproduces the four observed rates exactly. So the LPM’s interaction coefficient is the difference in gaps, in percentage points. (Their standard errors differ a little.)
  2. Near the ceiling (b0 = 4.6, the seminar’s audit), the percentage-point test almost always rejects and the log-odds test rarely does. With all rates in the middle (b0 = 2.5), both usually reject. With b0 = 1, the gap pushes West-African-sounding callers in far-right towns toward the floor, and the pattern reverses: now the log-odds test rejects more often. Same interaction on the log-odds scale in all three, yet the two tests disagree in different directions. Which one is “significant” depends on where the rates sit, which is one more reason to pick the scale from your question, not from the p-values. (Near the ceiling you may also see a warning or a huge coefficient: an audit in which no native-Italian-sounding caller was refused in one kind of town. That is separation, on the auxiliary slides.)

Part IV (optional): Non-collapsibility 🧱

⚠️ This part is optional, for you to work through on your own if you are interested. Martín will not cover it in the lab. It follows the seminar’s “What is a logit coefficient?” part: Mood (2010) and Buis (2017), both on the reading list.

Buis’s table, by hand 🧮

Does a child enter university, depending on whether a parent has a degree? Two countries, 400 children in each cell (Buis 2017). Parents’ degrees are equally common in both countries, so country is not a confounder.

buis <- tibble::tribble(
  ~country, ~degree, ~enters, ~not,
  "A",       0,       200,     200,
  "A",       1,       300,     100,
  "B",       0,       100,     300,
  "B",       1,       200,     200
)

A small function that turns counts into the two effect measures:

two_measures <- function(df) {
  p <- df %>%
    dplyr::group_by(degree) %>%
    dplyr::summarize(p = sum(enters) / sum(enters + not)) %>%
    dplyr::pull(p, name = degree)
  odds <- p / (1 - p)
  tibble::tibble(p_no_degree = p[["0"]], p_degree = p[["1"]],
                 difference = p[["1"]] - p[["0"]],
                 odds_ratio = odds[["1"]] / odds[["0"]])
}

buis %>% dplyr::filter(country == "A") %>% two_measures()
buis %>% dplyr::filter(country == "B") %>% two_measures()
buis %>% two_measures() # both countries pooled

The difference is .25 in each country and pooled: it is collapsible. The odds ratio is 3 in each country but 2.78 pooled: it is not. No confounding, no bias: pooling averages probabilities, and an average of probabilities is not an average of odds.

A simulation: add a covariate that has nothing to do with the treatment 🧪

A get-out-the-vote letter is randomized. Past turnout predicts voting strongly, and by randomization it is unrelated to the letter. We fit a logit with and without past turnout, and compute the letter’s coefficient and its average effect on the probability (by hand, with counterfactual predictions, as in Part II).

ame_by_hand <- function(model, data, variable) {
  p1 <- predict(model, newdata = dplyr::mutate(data, "{variable}" := 1), type = "response")
  p0 <- predict(model, newdata = dplyr::mutate(data, "{variable}" := 0), type = "response")
  mean(p1 - p0)
}

sim_letter <- function(n = 5000, b_past = 2.6) {
  d <- tibble::tibble(letter = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5), past = rbinom(n, 1, 0.4)) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(voted = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-2 + 0.45 * letter + b_past * past)))
  m_without <- glm(voted ~ letter, data = d, family = binomial)
  m_with <- glm(voted ~ letter + past, data = d, family = binomial)
  tibble::tibble(
    logit_without = coef(m_without)[["letter"]],
    logit_with = coef(m_with)[["letter"]],
    ame_without = ame_by_hand(m_without, d, "letter"),
    ame_with = ame_by_hand(m_with, d, "letter")
  )
}

sim_letter() # one experiment

One experiment could be a fluke. Let’s run 200, with purrr::map():

sims <- purrr::map(1:200, \(i) sim_letter()) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind()

sims %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("quantity", "model"), names_sep = "_") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(quantity = dplyr::recode(quantity, logit = "Logit coefficient",
                                         ame = "Average effect on the probability"),
                model = paste(model, "past turnout")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(value, fill = model)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, color = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~quantity, scales = "free") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#B9BEC5", "#1d375b")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The logit coefficient on the letter moves when we add past turnout, in almost every one of the 200 experiments, even though past turnout has nothing to do with the letter. The average effect on the probability stays where it was; it only gets a little more precise.

Activity 💡

  1. The data were generated with a letter coefficient of 0.45, conditional on past turnout. Which of the two logit coefficients recovers it? Is the other one “biased”?
  2. How much the coefficient moves depends on how strongly past turnout predicts voting. Use tidyr::expand_grid() and purrr::pmap() (or purrr::map()) to run 100 experiments for each of b_past = c(0, 1, 2.6, 4), and plot the average gap between logit_with and logit_without against b_past.
  3. Add the LPM coefficient of the letter, with and without past turnout, to sim_letter(). Does it move?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
# 1.
sims %>% dplyr::summarize(dplyr::across(everything(), mean))
# 2.
by_strength <- tidyr::expand_grid(b_past = c(0, 1, 2.6, 4), rep = 1:100) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(res = purrr::map(b_past, \(b) sim_letter(b_past = b))) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(res) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(b_past) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(coef_gap = mean(logit_with - logit_without),
                   ame_gap = mean(ame_with - ame_without))
by_strength
ggplot(by_strength, aes(b_past, coef_gap)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1d375b") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1d375b") +
  labs(x = "How strongly past turnout predicts voting (log-odds)",
       y = "Logit coefficient: with minus without past turnout") +
  theme_minimal()
# 3.
sim_letter_lpm <- function(n = 5000, b_past = 2.6) {
  d <- tibble::tibble(letter = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5), past = rbinom(n, 1, 0.4)) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(voted = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-2 + 0.45 * letter + b_past * past)))
  tibble::tibble(lpm_without = coef(lm(voted ~ letter, data = d))[["letter"]],
                 lpm_with = coef(lm(voted ~ letter + past, data = d))[["letter"]])
}

purrr::map(1:200, \(i) sim_letter_lpm()) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind() %>%
  dplyr::summarize(dplyr::across(everything(), mean))
  1. The model with past turnout recovers 0.45, because that is the effect we built in, conditional on past turnout. The model without it estimates a smaller number, but it is not biased: it is the effect on the odds for the whole population, a different quantity. Both are correct answers to different questions, which is exactly why logit coefficients from models with different covariates cannot be compared directly.
  2. With b_past = 0, past turnout predicts nothing and the two coefficients agree. The stronger the covariate, the larger the gap. The average effects on the probability barely move at any strength.
  3. The LPM coefficient does not move (beyond noise): differences in probabilities are collapsible.

Wrap-up 🎁

  • Maximum likelihood scores every candidate value by how probable it makes the observed data, and keeps the best. The curvature at the top gives the standard errors. glm() does this for you; optim() lets you do it for any log-likelihood you can write down.
  • The LPM, logit, and probit speak different languages. Compare them through the same quantity: predictions, comparisons (such as the AME), and slopes, computed from counterfactual predictions.
  • Slopes and comparisons by group show whether an effect differs across people, and you can test that difference directly. A coefficient table cannot show it.
  • An interaction in a logit depends on the scale. The coefficient answers a question about odds ratios; the difference in gaps answers a question about probabilities. Choose the scale from your question.
  • Optional Part IV: odds ratios are not collapsible. Adding a covariate that predicts the outcome moves the logit coefficient, even in a randomized experiment; differences in probabilities do not move.
  • R skills from today: writing a log-likelihood as a function, optimize() and optim() (with fnscale = -1 and hessian = TRUE), counterfactual predictions by changing a column and predicting again, the {marginaleffects} verbs (predictions(), avg_comparisons(), avg_slopes(), with by =, hypothesis =, and type =), and repeating a simulation with purrr::map() and purrr::list_rbind().
